title: Chickpea & Lentil Air-Fryer Bread
description: Category: Bread • Flourless • Gluten-free ingredients • Savoury loaf Important: These expanded directions clarify the method from the earlier recipe card. The quantities and approximate cooking time below have not been independently verified against a full transcript of the linked video. Check the video if an exact detail differs.
ingredients:
150 g (5.3 oz) lentils, soaked overnight
150 g (5.3 oz) dried chickpeas, soaked overnight
100 ml fresh water, divided: 50 ml for the lentils and 50 ml for the chickpeas
80 g (2.8 oz) ground flaxseed
1 tsp baking powder
A pinch of salt
Rosemary and ground black pepper, to taste
Optional topping: whole flaxseeds or sesame seeds
directions:
Detailed directions
Soak the legumes. Put the lentils in one bowl and the chickpeas in a second bowl. Cover each with plenty of cool
water; they will absorb water and swell. Leave to soak overnight. Keep them separate because they are blended
separately.
Drain and rinse. Pour off all the soaking water. Rinse the lentils and chickpeas under cool running water, then drain
very well. Do not use the soaking water in the batter; measure fresh water for blending.
Blend the lentils. Place the drained lentils in a blender with 50 ml fresh water. Blend, stopping to scrape down the
sides as needed, until the mixture is as smooth as your blender can make it. If it stalls, pause and scrape rather than
adding extra water straight away.
Blend the chickpeas. Transfer the drained chickpeas to the blender with the other 50 ml fresh water. Blend thoroughly,
scraping down the sides. The chickpea mixture may be thicker than the lentil mixture; aim for an even paste with no
large hard pieces.
Combine and season. Scrape both mixtures into a large bowl. Add the ground flaxseed, baking powder, salt, rosemary
and black pepper. Stir firmly until there are no dry pockets of flaxseed and the mixture is evenly combined.
Rest the batter. Leave the bowl for 20–40 minutes. During this rest, the ground flaxseed absorbs moisture and thickens
the mixture. After resting, it should be thick enough to mound on a spoon and shape; it should not pour like a thin
pancake batter.
Shape the loaf. Wet your hands or a spatula to reduce sticking. Gather the mixture into a loaf shape and smooth the
surface. Transfer it to an air-fryer-safe loaf pan or baking container that fits with room for air to circulate. Do not fill the
pan to the very top.
Add the topping. If desired, scatter flaxseeds or sesame seeds over the surface and gently press them on so they
adhere.
Air-fry. Preheat the air fryer if your model's instructions recommend it. Cook at 170°C (340°F) for approximately 1 hour,
as stated on the earlier card. Air fryers and pan sizes vary, so begin checking before the hour is up. If the top becomes
dark before the centre is cooked, shield it loosely only with an accessory approved for your air fryer; never let foil or
parchment touch the heating element or block airflow.
Check that it is cooked. The loaf should be firm and set rather than wet or paste-like in the middle. If the centre is still
soft or gummy, continue cooking in short increments and check again. A skewer may come out slightly moist because
this is a legume-based loaf, but it should not carry raw batter. If you have a food thermometer, use it as an additional
check, not as a substitute for confirming the centre is set.
Cool before slicing. Carefully remove the pan using heat-safe gloves. Let the loaf cool in the pan briefly, then turn it
out if it releases easily. Cool completely on a rack before cutting. This is important: the flaxseed and legume mixture
firms as it cools, and slicing while hot can make the centre seem gummy.
Serve and store. Slice with a sharp serrated knife. Store covered in the refrigerator and use within 3–4 days; freeze
slices with parchment between them for longer storage. Reheat or toast slices before serving. Discard if it develops an
off smell, mould or unusual texture.
Optional avocado-dill spread
Ingredients: 2 garlic cloves, 1 bunch fresh dill, ½ avocado and salt to taste.
Directions: Peel the garlic. Rinse and dry the dill, removing any very tough stems. Scoop the avocado flesh into a small
food processor or blender. Add garlic, dill and a little salt. Blend, scrape down the sides, and blend again until creamy.
Taste and adjust the salt. Serve on cooled slices of bread.
Recipe notes
The linked video’s exact pan dimensions, yield and detailed visual doneness cues were not confirmed when this PDF was prepared.
The cooking time is approximate; use the loaf’s texture and your air fryer’s behaviour as the guide. For a strictly gluten-free result,
check that the baking powder, seasonings and any toppings are certified gluten-free.

description: Category: Salads & Side Dishes | Makes: approximately 8 servings A classic creamy, sweet and tangy coleslaw with finely chopped cabbage, carrot and onion. For the best flavour, prepare it the night before.

title: Golden Puffy Fried Dough
description: Soft, airy rounds with a golden, lightly crisp outside Category: Bread / Fried Dough Yield: 8–10 rounds Time: About 2 hours A note about the source The supplied Facebook screenshot shows round pieces of dough frying in oil, with hot oil spooned over the tops. It does not show the ingredient list or method. This is a carefully reconstructed, pi n i-style yeast dough recipe based on the appearance; it may not be the exact creator's recipe.
ingredients:
500 g (about 4 cups) all-purpose flour, plus a little for shaping
300 ml (1¼ cups) warm water, approximately 38–40°C (100–104°F)
7 g (2¼ tsp) instant yeast
10 g (1¾ tsp) fine salt
10 g (2 tsp) sugar
15 ml (1 tbsp) neutral oil, for the dough
Neutral frying oil, enough for 2–3 cm (¾–1¼ in) depth in a wide heavy pan
directions:
1. Mix the dough. Stir the warm water, yeast and sugar together. Add the flour, salt and 1 tablespoon oil. Mix until a
shaggy dough forms.
2. Knead. Knead by hand for 8–10 minutes, or with a mixer and dough hook for 5–6 minutes, until smooth and elastic.
The dough should be soft and slightly tacky, not runny. Add flour a teaspoon at a time only if it is too sticky to handle.
3. First rise. Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise in a warm place for 60–90 minutes, until doubled.
4. Shape. Gently deflate the dough. Divide into 8–10 equal pieces. Shape into balls, cover and rest for 10 minutes. Flatten
each into a round about 1–1.5 cm ( n –½ in) thick. Keep the rounds covered while you work.
5. Heat the oil. Add oil to a wide, heavy frying pan to a depth of 2–3 cm. Heat to 170–175°C (340–350°F). Use a
thermometer if possible; avoid filling the pan more than halfway.
6. Fry. Carefully place 2–3 rounds in the oil, leaving room for expansion. Fry about 1½–2½ minutes on the first side. As in
the screenshot, spoon a little hot oil over the top to help it puff and set. Turn and fry another 1–2 minutes, until evenly
golden and cooked through. Adjust the heat to keep the oil near 170–175°C.
7. Drain and serve. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack or paper towels. Let the oil return to temperature
before frying the next batch.
Helpful tips
Do not overcrowd the pan; too many pieces lower the oil temperature and make the dough greasy.
If the outside browns before the centre cooks, lower the oil temperature slightly and make the next rounds a little thinner.
If the dough does not puff, check that it has risen well and that the oil is hot enough. Avoid pressing the rounds flat after
shaping.
For a savoury finish, serve warm with cheese, olives, eggs or soup. For a sweet version, dust with icing sugar or drizzle
with honey.
Food safety
Use a deep, stable pan and keep the handle turned inward. Lower dough gently away from you, keep water away from hot
oil, and never leave frying oil unattended. If the oil smokes, turn off the heat and let it cool; do not add water.

ingredients:
Two Old-Fashioned Pork Rib Recipes
Farmhouse salt-cured-style ribs and dry-seasoned hot-smoked BBQ ribs
Batch size for each recipe: 2.27 kg (5 lb) pork ribs. These are refrigerator seasoning cures for flavour, not
preservation cures. They contain no curing salt and do not make the ribs shelf-stable.

Recipe 1 – Traditional Farmhouse Salt-Cured-Style Ribs
Savoury, salt-forward ribs with a firmer farmhouse character and a pronounced wood-smoke flavour.
Ingredient Amount
Pork ribs 2.27 kg (5 lb)
Kosher salt 34 g
Brown sugar 10 g
Black pepper 8 g
Garlic powder 4 g
Onion powder 3 g
Ground mustard 3 g
Crushed bay leaf 1 g
Prepare and season
Remove the membrane from the bone side. Mix the salt, brown sugar, pepper, garlic, onion, mustard and bay leaf.
Rub evenly over both sides of the ribs.
Refrigerate
Place in a covered food-safe container or sealed bag and refrigerate at 4°C (40°F) or colder for 24–36 hours. Turn
once during this period. This short refrigerated seasoning step is for flavour only; it is not a shelf-stable cure.
Dry the surface
Remove the ribs, rinse off excess surface salt if desired, and pat dry. Place uncovered on a rack in the refrigerator
for 2–4 hours.
Smoke and finish
Smoke at 225°F (107°C), using hickory or oak, until tender. For food safety, whole pork ribs must reach at least
145°F (63°C) followed by a 3-minute rest. For a tender barbecue-style texture, continue cooking to approximately
195–203°F (91–95°C), checking tenderness rather than relying on temperature alone.

Recipe 2 – Dry-Seasoned Hot-Smoked BBQ Ribs
A balanced savoury-sweet rub, applewood smoke and a tender barbecue finish.
Ingredient Amount
Pork ribs 2.27 kg (5 lb)
Kosher salt 27 g
Brown sugar 30 g
Black pepper 10 g
Paprika 8 g
Garlic powder 5 g
Onion powder 4 g
Mustard powder 3 g
Cayenne pepper (optional) 1 g
Prepare and season
Remove the membrane. Mix all dry ingredients and coat both sides of the ribs evenly.
Refrigerate
Place in a covered food-safe container or sealed bag and refrigerate at 4°C (40°F) or colder for 12–24 hours. This is
a flavour seasoning step, not a preservation cure.
Dry the surface
Remove the ribs and pat dry. Place uncovered on a rack in the refrigerator for 2–4 hours.
Hot smoke
Preheat the smoker to 225°F (107°C). Smoke with applewood; a little cherrywood can be added. Smoke until the
bark is a deep mahogany colour.
Wrap if desired
Once the bark has developed, wrap in butcher paper or foil if you want a softer exterior and faster finish. Continue
cooking until tender, commonly around 195–203°F (91–95°C).
Optional glaze
Brush lightly with barbecue sauce during the final 15–20 minutes, then rest briefly before serving.
Food-safety and storage notes
Keep raw ribs refrigerated at 4°C (40°F) or colder during seasoning. These recipes do not preserve meat: do not hang, air-dry at room
temperature, cold-smoke for storage, or store unrefrigerated. Cook promptly after the seasoning step. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and
use within 3–4 days, or freeze. If you want genuinely preserved, long-term dry-cured ribs, use a validated process designed for the exact cut,
thickness, cure formulation and drying conditions; do not improvise curing-salt quantities.

title: Traditional Old-Fashioned Hot-Smoked Dry-Cured Bacon
description: Skinless pork belly • traditional salty flavour • hot smoked Batch size: 2.27 kg (5 lb) skinless pork belly Flavour: savoury, traditional bacon with applewood smoke and optional light hickory.
ingredients:
Ingredient Amount
Skinless pork belly 2.27 kg (5 lb)
Kosher salt 45 g
Brown sugar 20 g
Prague Powder #1 (6.25% sodium nitrite) 4.35 g
Coarsely ground black pepper 8 g
Garlic powder 3 g
Onion powder 2 g
Critical curing note: For this exact 2,270 g batch, 4.35 g of Prague Powder #1 containing 6.25% sodium nitrite calculates to
approximately 120 ppm ingoing sodium nitrite. Weigh the belly and curing salt accurately. Do not substitute Prague Powder #2,
ordinary pink salt, or a different curing blend. If your curing product has a different formulation, use its manufacturer’s tested bacon
recipe.
directions:
1. Prepare the belly
Trim loose edges, remove any remaining skin, pat dry and weigh the skinless belly. Divide into pieces of
reasonably even thickness if needed.
2. Mix and apply the cure
Mix the salt, brown sugar, black pepper, garlic powder and onion powder evenly. Separately verify the weighed
Prague Powder #1 amount, then distribute the complete cure mixture evenly over every surface of the belly. Place
in a food-safe curing bag or suitable sealed container and refrigerate.
3. Cure under refrigeration
Keep at 1–4°C (34–40°F), turn the package daily, and follow a validated thickness-based curing schedule for the
actual thickness of the belly. A typical home bacon process may take about 5–7 days, but thickness and the tested
recipe determine the required time; do not rely on a fixed number of days alone.
4. Rinse and dry
Remove the belly and rinse thoroughly under cold running water to remove surface cure. Pat dry. Place on a rack
over a tray, uncovered in the refrigerator for 12–24 hours, until the surface is dry and slightly tacky (the pellicle).
5. Hot smoke
Preheat the smoker to about 225°F (107°C). Use applewood; add a little hickory if you prefer a stronger smoke.
Place the belly on the rack and smoke until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C),
measured with a reliable thermometer. The time may be roughly 2–4 hours but depends on thickness and smoker
performance.
6. Chill
Remove from the smoker and refrigerate promptly in a shallow container or on a rack. Once thoroughly chilled,
wrap or vacuum seal and refrigerate overnight before slicing.
7. Slice and store
Slice about 2–3 mm for thin bacon, 3–4 mm for regular slices, or 5–6 mm for thick-cut bacon. Keep refrigerated at
4°C or colder and use within 7 days, or freeze in meal-size portions for best quality for about 4 months. Thaw in the
refrigerator.
Food-safety reminders
Keep raw pork refrigerated throughout curing. Use a calibrated scale for curing salt and a food thermometer for
smoking. Do not taste the cure mixture. Hot-smoked bacon is not shelf-stable; keep it refrigerated or frozen. If the
pork has been cured using an incorrect amount or an unknown curing blend, do not proceed on the assumption
that rinsing will correct it.
Reference: CFIA, Preventive control recommendations on the use of nitrites in the curing of meat products; Ontario Meat Plant
Guidelines; Oregon State University Extension, Making cured bacon at home (PNW 784). This home recipe is not a substitute for a
validated commercial process.

title: Homemade Maple Syrup Mead
description: Category: Mead (Acerglyn) Batch: 1 US gallon (3.8 L) Estimated alcohol: approximately 11–13% ABV, depending on starting gravity and final dryness. Yield: about 4 bottles.
ingredients:

1 packet Lalvin D-47 or 71B wine yeast
Yeast nutrient, according to package directions and a staged schedule if specified
½ tsp pectic enzyme (optional)

Acid blend, optional; adjust to taste after fermentation

Sanitize the fermenter, spoon, airlock, siphon and all equipment that will touch the mead.

Fit an airlock and ferment around 18–22°C (64–72°F), following the yeast's temperature guidance.

Allow fermentation to finish; secondary fermentation may take several weeks or longer. Use a hydrometer
8
and confirm stable readings before bottling.

9

title: Gordon Ramsay’s Yorkshire Puddings
description: Makes 8 large puddings • Prep: 10 minutes • Rest: 1 hour • Bake: about 15 minutes
ingredients:
3 large eggs
125 g plain flour (all-purpose flour)
½ teaspoon sea salt
150 ml whole milk
Vegetable oil or beef dripping, for the tins (about 2 teaspoons per large cup)
directions:
Beat the eggs in a mixing bowl with a whisk.
1
Sift the flour and salt together. Gradually whisk the flour into the eggs until you have a smooth batter.
2
Whisk in the milk. Cover and leave the batter to rest at room temperature for about 1 hour.
3
Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan / 425°F). Add about 2 teaspoons of oil or beef dripping to each
4
compartment of two 4-hole Yorkshire pudding tins.
Put the tins in the oven for 12–15 minutes, until the fat is very hot. This is essential for a good rise.
5
Stir the batter and pour it into a jug. Carefully, while the tins are still in the oven or right beside it, pour
6
batter into the hot fat. The batter should sizzle. Fill each compartment roughly halfway to two-thirds full.
Return the tins to the oven immediately. Bake for about 15 minutes, until well risen, golden and crisp.
7
Do not open the oven door while they bake.
Serve immediately with roast beef and gravy.
8
Gordon’s tips for a good rise
Rest the batter for at least 1 hour. • The oil or dripping must be piping hot before the batter goes in. • Work
quickly and keep the oven door closed during baking. • For 14–16 smaller puddings, use a deep muffin tin
with about 1 teaspoon of oil per cup and bake for 12–15 minutes.
Source: Gordon Ramsay Restaurants, “Yorkshire Puddings” (official recipe).

title: The Barrel Restaurant–Style Panzerotti
description: A home copycat inspired by The Barrel Restaurant . Its menu describes a generously filled panzerotti with a golden crust, served with tomato meat sauce for dipping.
ingredients:
Makes 4 large panzerotti
Dough

500 g Bread Flour
(All purpose flour +12g of vital wheat gluten)
325 g lukewarm water
7 g instant yeast
10 g fine salt
10 g sugar
20 g olive oil



Classic Barrel-style filling (for 4)
200 g low-moisture mozzarella, shredded
•
100 g pepperoni, chopped
•
100 g mushrooms, finely sliced and sautéed until their moisture evaporates, then cooled
•
75 g green pepper, finely diced
•
4–6 tbsp thick pizza sauce (use sparingly; serve more on the side)
•
Optional: 2 tbsp grated Parmesan
•
Tomato meat sauce for dipping
1 tsp olive oil
•
150 g lean ground beef
•
½ small onion, finely minced
•
1 garlic clove, minced
•
1 cup passata or crushed tomatoes
•
1 tbsp tomato paste
•
½ tsp dried oregano, plus salt and pepper to taste
•
Method
Make the dough: Stir water, yeast and sugar together. Mix in flour and salt until a rough dough forms. Knead
1
7–9 minutes until smooth and elastic. Knead in olive oil. Cover.
Rise: Let rise at room temperature for 60–90 minutes, until doubled.
2
Make the dipping sauce: Brown beef in olive oil with onion. Add garlic for 30 seconds. Stir in passata, tomato
3
paste and oregano. Simmer gently 20–25 minutes until thick. Season and keep warm.
Prepare the filling: Sauté mushrooms until no liquid remains. Cool completely. Combine with pepperoni,
4
green pepper and mozzarella. Keep the filling fairly dry.
Divide and rest: Divide dough into 4 equal portions (about 215 g each). Shape into balls, cover and rest
5
15–20 minutes.
Fill: Roll each ball into a 20–22 cm (8–8½ inch) circle. Put one-quarter of the filling on one half, leaving a 2 cm
6
border. Add only 1–1½ tbsp thick pizza sauce.
Seal firmly: Lightly moisten the edge with water. Fold into a half-moon, press out trapped air, press the seam
7
firmly and crimp or fold the edge. Check for holes and keep filling away from the seam.
Fry for a classic golden crust: Heat 5–6 cm (2–2½ inches) of neutral oil to 175°C (350°F). Fry one at a time,
8
turning, about 3–4 minutes total until deeply golden and cooked through. Keep oil close to temperature; do not
crowd the pot. Drain on a wire rack.
Serve: Rest 3–5 minutes, then serve with warm tomato meat sauce for dipping.
9
Other Barrel-style choices
Hawaiian: Replace the pepperoni, mushrooms and green pepper with diced ham and well-drained pineapple;
•
keep mozzarella.

Greco: Use black olives, cooked and drained ground beef, crumbled feta and green pepper.
•
Important tips: Low-moisture mozzarella and thoroughly cooked mushrooms help prevent leaks. Do not overfill. The
restaurant’s published menu confirms the filling combinations and meat-sauce dip, but not whether its crust is fried or baked;
frying here is a traditional panzerotti-style copycat method.

title: Cherry Liqueur
description: Homemade Italian-Style Cherry Liqueur Yield Infusion Finish About 1 litre 20–30 days Rest 2–4 weeks
ingredients:
500 g ripe fresh cherries
500 ml vodka (40% alcohol)
300 g white sugar
250 ml water
1 strip lemon zest
1 small stick cinnamon (optional)
½ bean vanilla bean (optional)
1. Prepare the cherries
Wash the cherries and remove the stems and pits. Discard any damaged or mouldy fruit. Do not crack or crush the pits.
2. Infuse
Put the pitted cherries in a clean glass jar. Add the vodka, lemon zest and optional cinnamon or vanilla. Make sure the
fruit is covered by the alcohol. Seal the jar and keep it in a cool, dark place for 20–30 days. Gently turn the jar every few
days.
3. Strain
Strain through a fine-mesh strainer, then filter through cheesecloth or a coffee filter for a clearer liqueur. Do not
squeeze the fruit if you want a clearer result.
4. Make the syrup
Combine the sugar and water in a saucepan. Warm gently, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Cool completely.
5. Blend and bottle
Gradually stir the cooled syrup into the cherry-infused vodka. Taste and adjust sweetness if desired. Pour into clean
bottles and seal.
6. Mature
Let the bottled liqueur rest for 2–4 weeks so the flavours can mellow. Keep refrigerated after bottling.
Serving Suggestions
Serve well chilled in small cordial glasses. It is also delicious over vanilla ice cream, spooned over chocolate desserts,
or added in a small splash to sparkling wine.
Storage & Safety
LIQUORE DI CILIEGIE • HOMEMADE RECIPE
Use clean equipment and commercially produced 40% vodka. Keep the fruit covered during infusion. Refrigerate the finished liqueur. This
homemade recipe has not been tested for shelf stability, so do not assume it can be stored indefinitely at room temperature. Discard if there
are signs of spoilage or if storage conditions are uncertain. Do not use cracked or crushed cherry pits; the kernels contain compounds that
can release cyanide.

title: Banana Liqueur
description: Italian-Style Creamy Banana Liqueur Batch Serving Storage About 1 litre Serve well chilled Refrigerate promptly
ingredients:
3 ripe bananas
400 ml vodka
250 ml 10% cream
300 ml milk
150 g granulated sugar
1 tsp saffron (or a small amount of turmeric for colour)
1. Prepare the bananas
Peel the bananas and cut them into small pieces.
2. Blend the dairy and fruit
Place the bananas, milk and cream in a blender. Blend until completely smooth.
3. Add sugar and colour
Add the sugar and saffron. Blend until the sugar is dissolved and the mixture is evenly combined. If using turmeric
instead, use only a small pinch at first; it is mainly for colour and has a stronger flavour.
4. Add the vodka
Slowly add the vodka and blend briefly until combined.
5. Strain and bottle
For a smoother drink, pass the mixture through a fine-mesh strainer. Transfer to clean, food-safe bottles, leaving a little
headspace.
6. Chill
Refrigerate immediately. Shake gently before serving, as natural settling may occur.
Serving Suggestions
Serve very cold in small cordial glasses. It can also be poured over vanilla ice cream or used as a dessert sauce.
Important Storage & Food Safety
Keep refrigerated at 4°C (40°F) or colder. This recipe contains fresh banana and dairy. The suggested two-week shelf life has not been
validated as safe, so do not assume it will keep safely for two weeks. Make small batches, keep it cold, and use promptly. Discard if storage
conditions are uncertain or there are signs of spoilage. Freezing in suitable containers may help preserve it longer; leave headspace for
LIQUORE ALLA BANANA • HOMEMADE RECIPE
expansion and thaw in the refrigerator.

title: Strawberry Liqueur
description: Traditional Italian-Style Strawberry Liqueur Yield Infusion Resting About 1 litre 20–30 days 2–4 weeks
ingredients:
500 g fresh, ripe strawberries
500 ml vodka (40% alcohol)
350 g white sugar
350 ml water
1 strip lemon zest (optional)
½ bean vanilla bean (optional)
1. Prepare the strawberries
Wash the strawberries and dry them thoroughly. Remove the green tops and cut the berries into quarters.
2. Infuse the alcohol
Place the strawberries in a clean glass jar. Pour in the vodka. Add the lemon zest and vanilla, if using. Seal the jar and
keep it in a cool, dark place for 20–30 days. Gently turn or shake the jar every few days.
3. Strain
Pour the infusion through a fine-mesh strainer. Filter again through cheesecloth or a coffee filter for a clearer liqueur. Do
not squeeze the fruit if clarity is important.
4. Make the syrup
Combine the sugar and water in a saucepan. Warm gently, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Do not boil vigorously. Cool
the syrup completely.
5. Combine and bottle
Gradually stir the cooled syrup into the strawberry-infused vodka. Taste and adjust sweetness if desired. Pour into clean
glass bottles and seal.
6. Mature
Let the bottled liqueur rest for 2–4 weeks so the flavours can mellow and blend. Keep refrigerated after bottling.
How to Serve
Serve well chilled in small cordial glasses. It is also lovely poured over vanilla ice cream, added in a small splash to
sparkling wine, or drizzled over fresh strawberries.
Italian Kitchen Note

Use very ripe, fragrant strawberries for the fullest fruit flavour. This recipe uses 40% vodka; do not substitute a
lower-proof drink without adjusting the method.
Storage and safety: Use clean jars and bottles, keep the infusion sealed and away from heat and light, and refrigerate the finished liqueur.
This homemade recipe has not been tested for shelf stability; do not assume it can be stored indefinitely at room temperature.

title: Homemade Croissant Dough
description: Yield: About 12 croissants
ingredients:
Ingredient Volume Approx. weight
All-purpose flour 4 cups about 500 g
Sugar ¼ cup about 50 g
Active dry yeast 1 packet (2¼ tsp) about 7 g
Salt 1½ tsp about 9 g
Warm milk 1¼ cups about 300 g
Unsalted butter, softened 2 tbsp about 28 g
Unsalted butter, cold (for laminating) 1 cup 227 g
directions:
1. Mix the warm milk, sugar and yeast in a large bowl. Let stand for 5–10 minutes, until foamy.
2. Add the flour, salt and softened butter. Mix until a dough forms, then knead briefly, about 3–5 minutes, until smooth.
Do not overwork.
3. Shape into a rectangle, wrap and refrigerate for about 1 hour, or until chilled and firm.
4. Place the cold laminating butter between two sheets of parchment. Pound and roll it into a flat rectangle about ½ inch
thick. Chill until firm but still bendable.
5. Roll the chilled dough into a rectangle roughly twice as long as the butter block. Place the butter on one half and fold
the other half over it, sealing the edges so the butter is enclosed.
6. Roll gently into a long rectangle. Fold it into thirds like a letter. Wrap and chill for 30–45 minutes. Repeat the rolling and
letter-folding two more times, chilling between folds. Keep the dough and butter cool; if butter starts to soften or squeeze
out, refrigerate before continuing.
My Recipe Book • Homemade Dough Collection Page 1
7. After the final fold, wrap and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, preferably overnight.
8. Roll the dough into a large rectangle about ¼ inch thick. Cut long triangles, make a small notch in the wide end if
desired, then roll each triangle toward its point. Curve the ends slightly.
9. Place on a lined baking sheet, leaving room to expand. Cover loosely and proof in a cool place until noticeably puffy,
about 1½–2½ hours. Do not let the butter melt.
10. Brush gently with egg wash if desired. Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 15–20 minutes, until deeply golden and crisp. Cool
on a rack.
Recipe note: Croissant dough needs cool resting time between folds. The finished layers should be distinct and the croissants
should be well browned before removing from the oven.

title: Homemade Puff Pastry Dough
description: Yield: Enough for 1 large sheet of pastry or several smaller pastries
ingredients:
Ingredient Volume Approx. weight
All-purpose flour 2½ cups about 315 g
Salt 1 tsp about 6 g
Cold unsalted butter, divided 1 cup 227 g
Ice-cold water ½ cup about 120 g
directions:
1. Whisk the flour and salt together in a large bowl.
2. Cut about 2 tablespoons of the cold butter into the flour until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.
3. Add the ice-cold water gradually, mixing just until a rough dough forms. Do not knead. Shape into a square, wrap and
chill for 30 minutes.
4. Place the remaining cold butter between parchment sheets and tap or roll it into a flat square about ½ inch thick. Chill
until firm but pliable.
5. Roll the dough into a square large enough to enclose the butter. Place the butter in the centre and fold the dough over
it, sealing the edges.
6. Roll gently into a long rectangle. Fold into thirds like a letter. Turn the dough a quarter turn, wrap and chill for 30
minutes.
7. Repeat the rolling, folding and chilling process 4 more times, keeping the dough cold and lightly dusting the work
surface with flour as needed. Brush away excess flour before folding.
8. After the final fold, wrap and chill for at least 1 hour before using. Roll to the thickness required by your recipe.
9. Bake shaped puff pastry on a cold baking sheet in a fully preheated oven. A common starting point is 400–425°F
(200–220°C); baking time depends on size and filling. Bake until well risen, crisp and golden.

Recipe note: Keep the butter in distinct layers and avoid letting it soften. If the dough becomes sticky or butter begins to break
through, stop and chill it.

title: Homemade Pizza Dough
description: Yield: About 2 medium pizzas
ingredients:
Ingredient Volume Approx. weight
All-purpose or bread flour 3½ cups about 440 g
Salt 1½ tsp about 9 g
Sugar 2 tsp about 8 g
Active dry yeast 1 packet (2¼ tsp) about 7 g
Warm water 1½ cups about 355 g
Olive oil 2 tbsp about 27 g
directions:
1. Stir the warm water, sugar and yeast together. Let stand for 5–10 minutes, until foamy.
2. Add the flour and salt. Mix until a shaggy dough forms.
3. Add the olive oil and knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. If sticky, add flour a tablespoon at a time; if dry,
add water a teaspoon at a time.
4. Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover and let rise for about 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
5. Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and divide into 2 portions. Shape into balls, cover and rest for 20–30
minutes.
6. Stretch or roll each ball into a pizza round. Add sauce, cheese and toppings, leaving a border around the edge.
7. Bake on a preheated pizza stone or baking sheet at 475–500°F (245–260°C) for about 8–15 minutes, depending on
oven temperature, thickness and toppings, until the crust is browned and the cheese is bubbling.
Recipe note: For more flavour, refrigerate the covered dough after its first mix for 12–48 hours. Bring it toward room
temperature before dividing and shaping.

title: Homemade Pie Crust Dough
description: Yield: One double-crust 9-inch pie, or two single crusts
ingredients:
Ingredient Volume Approx. weight
All-purpose flour 2½ cups about 315 g
Salt 1 tsp about 6 g
Sugar 1 tbsp about 12–13 g
Cold unsalted butter, cubed 1 cup 227 g
Ice-cold water 6–8 tbsp 90–120 g
directions:
1. Whisk the flour, salt and sugar together in a large bowl.
2. Add the cold cubed butter. Cut it into the flour with a pastry cutter or fingertips until you have a mixture with pea-sized
pieces and some larger flat flakes.
3. Drizzle in 6 tablespoons of ice water, tossing gently with a fork. Add more water, 1 tablespoon at a time, only until the
dough holds together when squeezed. Do not knead.
4. Divide into two equal portions for a double-crust pie. Shape each into a disk, wrap and refrigerate for at least 1 hour.
5. On a lightly floured surface, roll one disk into a circle large enough to line the pie plate. Turn the dough as you roll to
prevent sticking.
6. Add the filling. Roll out the second disk for the top crust, place over the filling and trim, seal and crimp the edges. Cut
vents in the top. For a single-crust pie, use one disk and follow the filling recipe.
7. Chill the assembled pie for 15–20 minutes before baking. Bake according to the pie filling recipe, since temperature
and time vary. For a blind-baked empty crust, line with parchment and pie weights and bake at 375°F (190°C) for about
20–25 minutes, removing weights near the end to brown.
Recipe note: Keep the butter and water cold, and handle the dough as little as possible for a tender, flaky crust.

title: Cinnamon Roll Dough
description: Yield: 9–12 rolls
ingredients:
Ingredient Volume Approx. weight

Instant or active dry yeast ¼ tsp about 0.8 g

3. Add the flour and salt. Mix to form a soft dough, then knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and stretchy. Add a

4. Place in a lightly greased bowl, cover and rise for 1–1½ hours, until doubled.
5. Roll into a rectangle. Spread with softened butter and sprinkle evenly with a filling of brown sugar and cinnamon.
6. Roll up from the long side and cut into 9–12 rolls. Arrange in a greased baking pan with a little space between

7. Cover and rise for 30–45 minutes, until puffy. Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 22–25 minutes, until golden and baked

title: Bagel Dough
description: Yield: 6–8 bagels
ingredients:
375g Bread flour or all-purpose flour
177 g warm water
0.8 g zeast
12–13 g sugar
3 g salt
2 g baking powder (optional)
directions:
1. Stir the warm water and yeast together; let stand for 5 minutes if using active dry yeast.
2. Add the flour, sugar, salt and optional baking powder. Mix to a stiff dough.
3. Knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. If too dry to come together, add water a teaspoon at a time.
4. Cover and rise for about 1 hour, until slightly puffy. It may not fully double.
5. Divide into 6–8 pieces. Shape each into a tight ball, poke a hole through the centre and gently stretch into a ring.
Rest for 10–15 minutes while the water heats.
6. Bring a wide pot of water to a gentle boil. Add 1 tablespoon sugar to the water if desired. Boil bagels for 30–45
seconds per side, working in batches. Drain well.
7. Place on a lined baking sheet. Add toppings while damp, if desired. Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 18–22 minutes,
until deeply golden. Cool before slicing.

cinnamon near the end of kneading.

title: Rustic No-Knead
description: Garlic Herb Bread Crisp golden crust • Soft, fragrant centre • Long, slow rise Yield: 1 round loaf Oven: 450°F (230°C) Rise: 12–18 hours
ingredients:
3 cups all-purpose flour
1½ tsp salt
½ tsp instant yeast
1½ cups warm water (about 100°F / 38°C)
4 garlic cloves, minced
2 tbsp olive oil
2 tbsp chopped fresh herbs (rosemary, thyme, parsley, or a mixture)
directions:
1. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, salt, and instant yeast. Stir until evenly distributed.
2. Add the minced garlic and chopped herbs, mixing them into the dry ingredients.
3. Pour in the warm water and olive oil. Stir with a wooden spoon until a sticky, shaggy dough forms. Do not
knead.
4. Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap or a clean kitchen towel. Let rise at room temperature for 12–18
hours, until bubbly and roughly doubled in size.
5. Lightly flour a work surface and gently turn out the dough. Fold the edges toward the centre a few times to

title: Sourdough Bread with All-Purpose & Durum Flour
description: A naturally leavened loaf combining all-purpose flour for a tender structure with finely ground durum flour for golden color, a gentle wheat sweetness, and a pleasantly chewy crumb. Yield: 1 medium-large loaf | Oven: 450°F (232°C) | Cold proof: 8–14 hours
ingredients:
100 g active sourdough starter at 100% hydration
350 g all-purpose flour
150 g finely ground durum flour
360 g water total: begin with 340 g and hold back 20 g
10 g fine sea salt
directions:
Make sure the starter is active, bubbly, and near its peak.
1
In a large bowl, combine the starter with 340 g of the water. Stir to loosen the starter.
2
Add the all-purpose flour and durum flour. Mix until all the flour is hydrated and no dry patches remain. Cover and
3
rest for 30–45 minutes.
Dissolve or sprinkle the 10 g salt over the dough. Work it in by pinching and folding. If the dough feels firm or
4
difficult to work, add some or all of the reserved 20 g water gradually, a little at a time. Durum flour absorption
varies, so do not add it automatically.
Bulk ferment at room temperature. During the first 2 hours, perform 3–4 sets of stretch-and-folds or coil folds,
5
spaced about 30 minutes apart. Keep the dough covered between folds.
Continue bulk fermentation until the dough looks smoother and aerated, has visible bubbles, and has risen
6
approximately 40–60%. Depending on room temperature and starter strength, this may take roughly 4–7 hours
total from mixing.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Pre-shape gently into a round and rest for 15–20 minutes. Shape
7
into a taut boule or oval, taking care not to tear the surface.
Place seam-side up in a well-floured banneton or a bowl lined with a floured towel. Cover and refrigerate for 8–14
8
hours.
Preheat a Dutch oven with its lid inside at 450°F (232°C) for at least 30 minutes.
9
Turn the cold dough onto parchment, seam-side down. Score the loaf with a sharp blade. Carefully lower it into the
10
hot Dutch oven and cover.
Bake covered for 25 minutes. Remove the lid and bake another 20–25 minutes, until the crust is deeply golden
11
brown.
Transfer to a wire rack and cool for at least 2 hours before slicing.
12
Baker's Notes
Water adjustment: Start with 340 g. Add the reserved water gradually only if the dough feels firm. The final dough
should feel supple and slightly tacky, not soupy.
Durum flour: Fine durum flour can absorb water differently depending on grind and brand. Give the flour time to
hydrate before deciding whether to add the reserved water.
Fermentation: Use the dough's rise, bubbles, and feel rather than the clock alone. Avoid waiting for a full doubling
if the dough is already very airy and delicate.
Hydration calculation: With a 100%-hydration starter, the formula has about 550 g total flour and 390–410 g total
water, or approximately 71–75% overall hydration.

title: Basic Artisan Sourdough Bread (same day)
description: A naturally leavened artisan loaf with a chewy crumb and crisp, deeply browned crust. This formula is approximately 70% hydration, based on the added water and flour. Yield: 1 large loaf | Hydration: about 70% | Cold proof: 8–16 hours
ingredients:
150 g active sourdough starter (100% hydration; bubbly and near peak)
500 g bread flour (about 3½ cups; weighing is more accurate)
350 g water (about 1½ cups), preferably cool or room temperature
10 g salt (about ½ tablespoon)
Optional starter feed, if needed: 50 g starter + 50 g warm water + 50 g flour. Feed and allow to become active
before measuring 150 g for the dough.
directions:
Check that the starter is active, bubbly, and near its peak. If it needs feeding, use the optional feed and wait until
1
it has risen and become lively.
In a large bowl, stir 150 g starter into 350 g water. Add 500 g bread flour and mix until no dry flour remains. Cover
2
and rest for 30–45 minutes.
Sprinkle the 10 g salt over the dough. Work it in with damp hands, pinching and folding until evenly distributed.
3
Perform 4 sets of stretch-and-folds, about 30 minutes apart. For each set, lift one edge of the dough, stretch it
4
upward without tearing, and fold it over the center. Turn the bowl and repeat on all four sides.
Continue bulk fermentation until the dough has risen roughly 50–75%, looks aerated, shows bubbles along the
5
sides, and has a slightly domed surface. This may take about 4–7 hours from mixing, depending on dough
temperature and starter strength.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Gently pre-shape into a round and rest uncovered for 15–20
6
minutes. Shape into a taut boule without pressing out all the gas.
Place seam-side up in a well-floured banneton or a bowl lined with a floured tea towel. Cover and refrigerate for
7
8–16 hours.
Place a Dutch oven with its lid in the oven and preheat to 450°F (232°C) for at least 30 minutes.
8
Turn the cold dough onto parchment, seam-side down. Score the top with a sharp bread lame or knife. Carefully
9
lower it into the hot Dutch oven and replace the lid.
Bake covered for 25 minutes. Remove the lid and bake another 20–25 minutes, until the crust is a deep golden
10
brown.
Transfer to a wire rack and cool for at least 2 hours before slicing so the crumb can finish setting.
11
Baker's Notes
Hydration note: If the starter is 100% hydration, its flour and water are included in the true dough calculation.
With 150 g starter, the total flour is about 575 g and total water about 425 g, giving approximately 74% overall
hydration.
Bulk fermentation: The 4–7 hour estimate is only a guide. Use the dough's rise and texture as your guide; a cool
kitchen may take longer.
Handling sticky dough: Use damp hands for folds and a light dusting of flour for shaping. Avoid adding lots of
extra flour, which changes the dough.
Safe handling: Use care when loading and unloading the very hot Dutch oven.

title: Homemade Italian Bread
description: A simple yeast-raised bread with a tender, chewy crumb and golden crust. Shape as one large loaf or two smaller loaves. Yield: 1 large loaf or 2 smaller loaves | Prep: 20 minutes | Rise: 1½–2¼ hours | Bake: 25–35 minutes
ingredients:
3½ cups (437 g) bread flour, plus more if needed
2¼ teaspoons (7 g) instant yeast
1 tablespoon (12 g) granulated sugar, optional
1½ teaspoons (10 g) salt
1½ cups (360 ml) warm water, about 105–115°F (40–46°C)
directions:
In a large bowl, whisk together the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar (if using), and salt.
1
Add the warm water. Mix until a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains.
2
Knead by hand for 8–10 minutes, or in a stand mixer with a dough hook for about 5–7 minutes, until smooth
3
and elastic. The dough should be soft and slightly tacky. Add flour a tablespoon at a time only if it is too wet to
handle.
Place the dough in a lightly greased bowl. Cover and let rise in a warm, draft-free place for about 60–90
4
minutes, or until doubled in size.
Gently deflate the dough. Shape into one large oval loaf or divide and shape into two smaller loaves. Place on a
5
parchment-lined baking sheet.
Cover and let rise for 30–45 minutes, until noticeably puffy. Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
6
Use a sharp knife or bread lame to make 2–3 diagonal slashes about ¼ inch (6 mm) deep across the top.
7
Bake for 25–35 minutes, depending on loaf size, until deeply golden. The center should reach about 200–210°F
8
(93–99°C), if checking with an instant-read thermometer.
Transfer to a wire rack and cool for at least 30 minutes before slicing.
9
Baker's Notes
Water temperature: 105–115°F (40–46°C) is a practical range for instant yeast. Avoid water hotter than 120°F
(49°C).
Crustier loaf: For extra crust, place a sturdy heatproof pan on the lower oven rack while preheating. When the
bread goes in, carefully add about 1 cup of hot water to the pan and close the oven door. Keep your face and
hands clear of the steam. Remove the water pan after about 10 minutes if safe to do so.
Storage: Keep cooled bread in a paper bag or bread box for a crisper crust, or in an airtight bag for a softer
crust. Freeze sliced bread for longer storage.

title: Sourdough Buttermilk Biscuits
description: Tender, lightly sweet biscuits with a hint of vanilla and tang from sourdough starter. The dough is chilled before shaping to help the cold butter stay in pieces and create a tender crumb. Yield: about 8–10 biscuits | Prep: 20 minutes + chilling | Bake: 18–23 minutes
ingredients:
227 g (8 oz) sourdough starter at 100% hydration (discard or active; unfed discard is fine)
113 g (4 oz) buttermilk or kefir
1 large egg
113 g (4 oz) light or dark brown sugar, or white sugar
1 tablespoon vanilla extract
170 g (6 oz) all-purpose flour, plus a little extra for dusting
1 teaspoon coarse salt or ½ teaspoon fine salt
1 tablespoon baking powder
113 g (4 oz) very cold unsalted butter
Optional: raw sugar for topping
directions:
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
1
In a bowl, whisk together the sourdough starter, buttermilk or kefir, egg, sugar, and vanilla until smooth.
2
In a separate large bowl, whisk together the flour, salt, and baking powder.
3
Cut the very cold butter into small cubes, or grate it using the large holes of a box grater. Toss the butter through
4
the flour mixture, separating any clumps. Leave visible small pieces of butter; do not rub it in completely.
Pour the wet mixture into the dry ingredients. Fold gently with a spatula just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms.
5
Do not knead.
Cover and chill the dough for 30–45 minutes, until firmer. This dough is naturally soft; dust your hands and work
6
surface lightly with flour rather than adding large amounts of flour to the dough.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Gently pat it into a rectangle about ¾–1 inch (2–2.5 cm) thick. Fold
7
it in thirds like a letter, turn it a quarter turn, and gently pat it out again. Repeat once for a little layering, taking
care not to warm the butter.
Cut into 8–10 rounds or squares. Gather scraps gently and reshape once if needed. Place biscuits on the
8
prepared sheet with a little space between them. Brush tops lightly with buttermilk and sprinkle with raw sugar, if
desired.
Bake for 18–23 minutes, until risen and golden and the centers are fully baked. Cool on the pan for 5 minutes,
9
then transfer to a rack.
Helpful Notes
Starter: Use 100%-hydration starter (equal weights flour and water). Discard works well; the starter does not
need to be bubbly.
Texture: This is a soft, enriched biscuit dough because of the starter, buttermilk, egg, and sugar. Chilling is
important. If it is too sticky to handle after chilling, dust the outside lightly with flour.
Keep the butter cold: Work quickly and return the dough to the refrigerator for 10 minutes if the butter begins to
soften.
Serving: These are slightly sweet and vanilla-scented. Serve warm with butter, jam, or honey.

title: Sour Cream Butter Drop Biscuits
description: Soft, rich, tender biscuits with a lightly golden top. This version uses the full 16 oz of sour cream, so the dough will be very soft and is portioned as drop biscuits rather than rolled and cut. Yield: about 12–16 biscuits | Prep: 10 minutes | Bake: 20–25 minutes
ingredients:
2 cups self-rising flour

½ cup salted butter, softened to room temperature
Optional: 1–2 tablespoons melted butter for brushing after baking
directions:
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Lightly grease a 12-cup muffin tin or line a baking sheet with parchment. A
1
muffin tin helps the soft dough hold its shape.
In a large bowl, stir the softened butter until smooth. Mix in the sour cream until mostly combined.
2
Add the self-rising flour. Fold gently just until no dry pockets remain. The mixture will be thick, sticky, and
3
softer than traditional biscuit dough; avoid overmixing.
Spoon the dough into the prepared muffin cups, filling each about n to ¾ full. If using a baking sheet, drop
4
generous mounds of dough with space between them.
Bake for 20–25 minutes, until the tops are golden and the centers are set. Muffin-tin biscuits may need a few
5
extra minutes.

6

For traditional, cut biscuits: Use about 8 oz (1 cup) sour cream instead of the full 16 oz. Mix gently, turn

Doneness: Because ovens and sour cream thickness vary, check that the center is cooked through before

title: Homemade Durum Egg Pasta
description: Traditional fresh pasta • Approximately 2 servings Description A simple traditional pasta made with finely sifted durum flour, fresh eggs, and a little water. This firm, flavorful dough is suitable for noodles, fettuccine, and lasagna sheets.
ingredients:
2 teacups (approximately 200 g) finely sifted durum flour
2 large eggs
A splash of clean water, as needed
Extra durum flour for dusting
directions:
Prepare the flour: Place the sifted durum flour on a clean work surface or in a mixing bowl. Make a well in the

Add the eggs: Crack the two eggs into the well.
Mix: Using a fork, gradually incorporate the flour into the eggs.
Adjust moisture: Add a small splash of water if the dough feels too dry. Add only a teaspoon at a time.
Knead: Knead by hand for approximately 8–10 minutes, until smooth, firm, and elastic.
Rest: Wrap the dough tightly in plastic wrap and let rest for 30–45 minutes at room temperature.
Roll: Divide into manageable portions. Roll with a pasta machine or rolling pin until thin.
Cut: Cut into your preferred shapes, such as fettuccine, spaghetti, or lasagna sheets.
Dry slightly: Let freshly cut pasta rest for 15–30 minutes before cooking.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.
Add the fresh pasta and cook for approximately 2–4 minutes, depending on thickness.
Taste for doneness, drain, and toss immediately with your favorite sauce.

Durum flour absorbs moisture differently depending on how finely it is ground.

title: Homemade Stromboli Dough
description:
Stromboli is a popular Italian-American baked turnover made by rolling pizza dough or bread dough around a filling of cheeses, Italian cold cuts or meats, vegetables, and sometimes marinara sauce

Durum & All-Purpose Flour • Makes 1 large Stromboli
ingredients:
Ingredient Amount
Durum flour 135 g
All-purpose flour 195 g
Warm water (105–110°F) 270 g
Active dry yeast 7 g
Sugar 12 g
Olive oil 27 g
Fine sea salt 6 g
directions:
1. Activate the yeast: Mix the warm water, sugar and yeast. Let stand for 5–10 minutes, until foamy. If using

2. Combine: Mix the durum flour, all-purpose flour and salt. Add the yeast mixture and olive oil. Stir until a shaggy
dough forms.
3. Knead: Knead by hand for 7–9 minutes, or in a stand mixer for 5–6 minutes, until smooth and elastic. The
dough should be soft and slightly tacky.
4. First rise: Place in a lightly oiled bowl, turn to coat, cover and let rise in a warm place for 60–90 minutes, or until

5. Shape: Gently deflate and roll into a rectangle about 10 × 16 inches on a lightly floured surface.
6. Fill and roll: Add meats and cheeses in an even layer, leaving a border. Use sauce sparingly. Roll tightly into a

7. Second rest: Place seam-side down on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and rest for 20–30

8. Bake: Brush with egg wash if desired. Cut 3–4 small vents across the top. Bake at 400°F (204°C) for about

Durum flour gives the crust a golden color and pleasantly chewy bite. Avoid overfilling or using too much wet sauce, which can

title: Grandma-Style Wild Grape Must Starter
description: A naturally fermented grape-and-flour starter for rustic bread, rolls and enriched doughs. This is a practical home formula based on established wild-grape starter methods—not a verified word-for-word transcription of the linked video, whose full ingredient list and timings were not accessible. Part 1 — Make the wild grape water
ingredients:
1 lb (454 g) ripe red or purple grapes, preferably organically grown
Clean drinking water only if needed to loosen the crushed fruit (usually none)
Equipment
Clean glass or food-safe container of at least 2 litres, clean spoon, fine sieve, clean jar, breathable cloth or loosely fitted
lid.
directions:
1. Remove damaged or moldy grapes. Do not scrub the healthy grapes; their natural surface bloom may carry wild yeast.
If visibly dirty, rinse gently and drain.
2. Remove stems and crush grapes by hand in the clean container. Include juice, skins and pulp.
3. Cover with a clean cloth or loose lid; do not seal airtight. Keep at 70–78°F (21–26°C).
4. Stir twice daily, pushing floating skins back under the juice. Look for small bubbles, gentle fizz and a fruity, wine-like
aroma. This commonly takes 3–5 days, but temperature and fruit affect timing.
5. When actively bubbly, strain through a clean fine sieve. Keep the liquid; discard the solids.
Part 2 — Build the flour starter
Day 1
Mix 1 cup (240 g) strained fermented grape liquid with 1 cup (120 g) rye flour in a clean 1-quart jar. Stir to a thick
porridge. Mark the level, cover loosely and keep at 70–78°F (21–26°C) for about 24 hours.
Days 2–5
Keep 1 cup (about 240 g) of the mixture. Add ½ cup (110 g) water and 1 cup scant (110 g) rye flour; mix well. Repeat
every 24 hours. Once it becomes reliably active, you may use bread flour for feedings, or keep it on rye for a robust,
easy-to-see culture.
Ready signs
The starter has many bubbles throughout, smells pleasantly tangy/fruity (not rotten), rises noticeably after feeding and
repeats that rise over several feedings. It may take 4–7 days or longer. A single early burst of bubbles is not proof that it
is mature.
Part 3 — First rustic grape-starter loaf
Ingredients — 1 medium loaf
300 g active grape starter, bubbly and recently risen
300 g water, room temperature
500 g bread flour (or 400 g bread flour + 100 g whole-wheat flour)
10 g fine salt
1. Stir starter and water together. Add flour and mix until no dry flour remains. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
2. Add salt and knead or pinch it through. Rest 20–30 minutes.
3. Give the dough 3 sets of stretch-and-folds, 30 minutes apart.
4. Bulk ferment at 72–78°F (22–26°C) until expanded by roughly 50–75%, aerated and slightly domed. Depending on
starter strength and room temperature, this may take 4–8 hours or longer. Follow the dough, not the clock.
5. Shape gently. Place seam-side up in a floured banneton or towel-lined bowl. Cover and refrigerate 8–12 hours, or
proof at room temperature until puffy.
6. Preheat a covered Dutch oven to 450°F (232°C). Turn out and score the loaf. Bake covered 20 minutes, then
uncovered at 425°F (218°C) for 20–25 minutes, until deep golden and the centre is about 205–210°F (96–99°C). Cool at
least 2 hours before slicing.
Part 4 — Keeping the starter
Room-temperature routine: Keep a small amount and feed about once daily, or twice daily in a warm kitchen. A
dependable maintenance feed is 1 part starter : 2 parts water : 2 parts flour by weight (for example 25 g starter + 50 g
water + 50 g flour). Adjust the interval so it is fed before it sits collapsed and hungry for long periods.
Refrigerator routine: Feed, let it begin showing activity, then refrigerate loosely covered. Refresh about weekly. Before
baking, give it 1–2 room-temperature feedings until it rises predictably.
For sweet doughs: Build a separate levain with bread flour and feed it once or twice before use so the grape/rye
character is milder. Sweet, buttery doughs ferment more slowly; allow extra time and judge by volume and softness, not
a fixed schedule.
Troubleshooting and food safety
No bubbles after 5 days: move it to a steady warm spot (not hot), stir twice daily and allow more time. If there is still no
activity, restart with fresh grapes.
Thin liquid or separation: stir and continue regular feedings; use a thicker flour feed if it is consistently runny.
Pink, orange, fuzzy growth, or a putrid/rotting smell: discard the entire batch and clean the equipment. Do not scrape
mold off or taste it.
Use clean jars and utensils; keep the fruit ferment covered from insects and stir the floating fruit down. Do not tightly
seal actively fermenting fruit because gas builds up.
Important notes
This is a wild culture: fermentation time, aroma and strength vary with grape variety, temperature and flour. The starter is
not guaranteed to behave exactly like commercial yeast or a mature wheat sourdough. For the linked video’s exact
quantities and sequence, a transcript or screenshots of its ingredient/method sections would be needed.
Reference notes
A documented wild-grape starter method uses unwashed grapes fermented 3–4 days, then strained grape liquid mixed
with rye flour and refreshed daily. A separate grape-yeast-water bread method uses fermented grape liquid mixed with
flour before baking. These support the general approach used here.
References: Wild Grape Sourdough Starter (Bread Daily recipe reproduced at ws64.com); Ancient Grape Must Bread
With Grape Yeast Water (Sew Historically).

title: Grandma-Style Homemade Durum Flour Calzones
description: Makes 4 individual calzones or pizzas • Golden, tender and pleasantly chewy
ingredients:
1 cup water (about 75°F / 24°C)
1 teaspoon yeast
1¼ cups all-purpose flour  (150g)
1 cup Durum flour. (130g)
1/2 tsp salt. (1 tsp Kosher salt)
1½ teaspoons olive oil 
Extra flour For dusting and kneading


1. Wake up the yeast
Pour the cool water into a mixing bowl. Sprinkle the active dry yeast over the water, stir gently, and let stand for 5–10
minutes. It should begin dissolving and may develop a little foam. If it does not foam, the yeast may be old; proceed only if
you know it is still active.

2. Make the dough
Add the all-purpose flour, durum flour, salt and olive oil. Stir with a wooden spoon until a rough, shaggy dough forms and no
dry flour remains. Turn the dough onto a lightly floured counter.

3. Knead
Knead by hand for 8–10 minutes: push the dough away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter turn, and
repeat. The finished dough should be smooth and elastic, slightly tacky but not sticky, and able to hold its shape.
If the dough is very sticky, add flour a tablespoon at a time. Avoid adding too much, which can make the crust tough.

4. First rise
Lightly oil a clean bowl. Place the dough inside and turn once to coat. Cover with a damp tea towel or plastic wrap. Let rise
at 75–80°F (24–27°C) for about 1–1½ hours, or until doubled in size and puffy. Use the dough’s appearance rather than the
clock alone.

5. Divide and rest
Gently press the air from the dough. Divide into 4 equal pieces and shape each into a ball. Cover and rest for 15–20
minutes. This relaxes the dough and makes it easier to roll.

6. Shape the calzones
Roll each ball into an 8–9-inch circle. Place filling on one half, leaving a ¾-inch border clear. Fold the other half over the
filling and press the edges firmly together. Crimp or fold the edges to seal. Cut 2 small steam vents in the top.
Do not overfill: excess filling can make the calzones split or leak during baking.

7. Bake
Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Place calzones on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush lightly with olive oil if
desired. Bake for 18–25 minutes, rotating the tray halfway through if your oven heats unevenly. They are ready when
deeply golden, firm underneath, and cooked through. Rest 5–10 minutes before cutting.
Filling ideas
Filling What to use
Classic cheese Mozzarella, ricotta, Parmesan and Italian seasoning
Pepperoni Mozzarella, pepperoni, a little pizza sauce and oregano
Sausage & mushroom Cooked Italian sausage, cooked mushrooms, mozzarella and garlic
Spinach & ricotta Well-drained cooked spinach, ricotta, mozzarella and Parmesan
Grandma’s baking tips
Chewier crust: Knead until the dough is smooth and elastic.
Softer crust: Brush with a little olive oil immediately after baking.
Crisper bottom: Preheat a pizza stone or steel and bake on it, following the manufacturer’s safe handling guidance.
More flavour: For an overnight dough, refrigerate it covered after kneading. The next day, let it warm until pliable and
puffy before dividing and shaping; allow extra time as needed.
Freezing: Freeze shaped, unbaked calzones individually. Bake from frozen at 400°F (205°C), adding time as needed and
checking that the centre is hot and fully cooked.
A note on the dough
Keep the full 1 cup of durum flour for its golden colour and pleasant bite. The dough should feel supple and slightly tacky;
add only enough extra flour to make it manageable.

title: Portuguese Stuffed Cabbage Rolls
description: Linguica, beef, mushrooms & tomato · Grandma-style kitchen directions Makes: about 8–10 rolls, depending on cabbage size & leaf size Oven: 350°F (175°C) · Bake: 30 minutes, covered Serve with: hot rice
ingredients:
Cabbage
1 large head green cabbage
1½ teaspoons salt, for the blanching water
Meat and vegetable filling
1¾ lb Portuguese linguica sausage, chopped
½ lb ground beef
1 cup chopped onion
1 cup chopped celery
1 cup mushrooms, chopped
½ cup olive oil
1 clove garlic, minced
1 teaspoon salt
¼ teaspoon black pepper
1 can (12 oz) whole tomatoes, crushed and drained; reserve the liquid
Before you begin
Have a large pot of salted water ready, a colander, a sauté pan, and a greased casserole dish. Separate the
cabbage leaves gently after blanching; the outer leaves are easiest to roll. If a leaf has a very thick centre rib,
carefully shave it thinner with a knife so it folds without tearing.
directions:
1. Soften the cabbage. Remove any damaged outer leaves. Place the whole cabbage in a large pot of salted
water. Bring to a boil, then lower to a simmer for about 2 minutes, or just until the outer leaves become flexible.
Drain and let cool enough to handle. Carefully peel off the leaves. Return the cabbage to the hot water briefly if
the inner leaves are still too firm.
2. Cook the filling. Heat the olive oil in a large sauté pan over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook for
2–3 minutes until it begins to soften. Add the linguica, ground beef, celery, mushrooms, garlic, crushed
tomatoes, salt and pepper. Cook gently for about 1 hour, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are tender
and the meat is thoroughly cooked. Keep the heat low enough that the mixture simmers gently rather than
sticking or scorching.
3. Use the small cabbage pieces. While the filling cooks, chop the smaller cabbage leaves and the thick
stems or ribs trimmed from the larger leaves. Stir these chopped pieces into the filling mixture and continue
cooking until tender.
4. Prepare to roll. Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Lightly grease a casserole dish. Let the filling cool just
enough to handle safely. Place about ½ cup filling near the base of each cabbage leaf (use less for smaller
leaves). Fold the two sides over the filling, then roll up from the stem end to make a neat parcel.
5. Arrange and bake. Place each roll seam-side down in the prepared casserole dish. Pour the reserved
tomato liquid evenly over the rolls. Cover the dish tightly with a lid or foil and bake for 30 minutes, until hot
throughout and the cabbage is tender.
6. Serve. Spoon some of the tomato juices over each roll. Serve warm over freshly cooked rice.
Grandma’s kitchen tips
Choose a large cabbage with broad, intact leaves; very small leaves are harder to fill.
Do not overfill. A snug ½ cup is the original recipe’s guide, but leaf size varies.
If the pan begins to dry during the long filling cook, lower the heat and add a small splash of water.
For food safety, cook the ground beef mixture to at least 160°F (71°C) before filling the leaves.
The rolls can be assembled ahead, covered and refrigerated; bake until thoroughly hot. If baking straight
from the refrigerator, allow extra time and check the centre.
Recipe note
The ingredient list and method through the filling, cabbage trimming, rolling, and baking were matched to the published recipe titled
“Portuguese Stuffed Cabbage Rolls” by Lizabeth (January 31, 2011). The screenshot provided ended mid-instruction; the missing
directions were recovered from that published recipe. The added kitchen tips are practical clarifications, not part of the original text.
Source: fantasticallyfamished.blogspot.com/2011/01/portuguese-stuffed-cabbage-rolls.html

title: Soft Homemade Hot Dog Buns
description: Pinch of Mint recipe • Makes 6 buns • About 2 hours 55 minutes PREP RISE / REST BAKE OVEN 10 min About 2 hours 25–30 min 180°C fan / 356°F fan
ingredients:
500 g Bread flour
7 g Instant yeast
15 g Caster sugar
6 g Salt
25 g Butter, melted
300 ml Milk, lukewarm / tepid
1 Egg, beaten, for glazing
directions:
1. Mix the dough
Put the flour in a large bowl. Add the yeast and sugar to one side and the salt to the other. Make a well in the centre; add
the melted butter and tepid milk. Mix until a dough forms.
2. Knead and first rise
Knead on a lightly floured work surface for 5–10 minutes, until smooth and shiny. Shape into a ball, return it to the bowl,
cover with a clean damp cloth and leave for about 1 hour, or until doubled in size.
3. Divide and rest
Turn out the dough and gently press out the air. Shape into a ball and divide into 6 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a
ball and let rest for 5 minutes.
4. Shape the buns
Flatten each ball into an oval. Turn it so the long side faces you, then roll it up towards you into a sausage shape,
pinching the seam as you go. Seal the seam and gently roll each bun to about 6–7 inches long.
5. Second rise
Place the buns on a parchment-lined baking tray, leaving space between them. Cover with a clean damp cloth and leave
to rise for about 1 hour.
6. Glaze and bake
Brush the tops with beaten egg. Bake in a preheated 180°C fan oven (356°F fan) for 25–30 minutes, until golden brown.
Helpful note: The recipe uses a fan oven temperature. If using a conventional oven, check your oven's conversion
guidance and watch the buns closely near the end of baking.
Source: Pinch of Mint – Hot Dog Buns (Tom; updated 17 August 2026). This PDF is a personal recipe-book copy of the ingredient list and
method.

title: Golden Italian Pizza Dough
description: Finely Ground Durum Flour • Chewy, golden crust Description A homemade Italian-style pizza dough made with finely ground durum flour and bread flour. Durum gives the crust its warm golden colour and gentle nutty flavour, while bread flour helps create a stretchy dough with a satisfying chew. Recipe Details Makes: 2 large (about 12-inch) pizzas Preparation: 25 minutes First rise: 1½–2 hours Optional cold ferment: 24–48 hours Bake: 500°F (260°C), about 7–12 minutes
ingredients:
3 cups (375 g) finely ground durum flour
1 cup (125 g) bread flour
1½ cups (355 ml) warm water
2 teaspoons salt
2 tablespoons olive oil
1 teaspoon honey or sugar
2 teaspoons instant yeast
directions:
1. Mix the dry ingredients
In a large bowl, combine the durum flour, bread flour and salt.
2. Add the liquids
Stir the yeast and honey into the warm water. Add to the flour with the olive oil. Mix until a rough dough
forms and no dry flour remains.
3. Knead
Knead for 10–12 minutes, by hand or with a mixer on low speed, until smooth and elastic. If the dough feels
very stiff, add water 1 teaspoon at a time. If very sticky, rest it for 10 minutes before adding any extra flour.
4. First rise
Place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at about 75–80°F (24–27°C) for 1½–2 hours, or until doubled
and puffy.
Golden Italian Pizza Dough • Page 1
5. Divide and rest
Divide into 2 equal pieces and shape into balls. Cover and rest for 20–30 minutes so the dough relaxes and
is easier to stretch.
6. Shape
Stretch each ball into a roughly 12-inch round. Avoid pressing all the air out of the rim. Place on a lightly
floured peel or baking sheet.
7. Top and bake
Add sauce, cheese and toppings. Bake on a thoroughly preheated pizza stone or steel at 500°F (260°C) for
about 7–12 minutes, until the crust is browned and the cheese is bubbling. Oven times vary; use the crust
colour as your guide.
Grandma's Baking Tips
For a chewier crust: Keep the bread flour in the recipe; it supports gluten development.
For deeper flavour: After kneading, cover and refrigerate the dough for 24–48 hours. Bring it back toward
room temperature for about 1–2 hours before shaping.
For a crisp bottom: Preheat the pizza stone or steel in the oven for at least 40 minutes.
For easy stretching: If the dough springs back, cover and rest it for another 10–15 minutes.
Water adjustment: Flour varies. Aim for a soft, supple dough, not a dry, firm ball.

title: Montana Durum Pizza Dough
description: Description A delicious, old-fashioned style pizza dough made with Montana durum flour and all-purpose flour. The durum flour gives the crust its beautiful golden colour and chewy texture, while the all-purpose flour helps create a light, airy rise. Yield: 2 pizza crusts Rising time: 1½–2 hours Cold fermentation: 1–2 days (optional) Baking temperature: 475–500°F
ingredients:
- 1½ cups Montana durum flour (for colour and chew)
- 1½ cups all-purpose flour (sifted; Rouge de Bordeaux recommended)

Sourdough option:

directions:

2. Make the dough: Add the durum flour, all-purpose flour, salt and olive oil. Gradually work in the flour until the dough feels soft and manageable.
3. Knead: Knead for approximately 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

7. Shape: Stretch each portion into a pizza crust. Add your favourite toppings.
8. Bake: Bake on a HOT pizza stone in a preheated 475–500°F oven or barbecue for approximately 10–15 minutes, until the crust is golden and crisp.

title: Commercial-Style English Muffins
description: Bakery-style • Makes 12–14 muffins • Stovetop griddle Soft and chewy inside with a lightly crisp, golden exterior and plenty of nooks and crannies.
ingredients:
Ingredient Amount
Bread flour 500 g (about 4 cups)
Warm water 275 g (about 1 n cups)
Warm milk 100 g (about n cup)
Instant yeast 7 g (2¼ tsp)
Sugar 25 g (2 tbsp)
Salt 10 g (about 1¾ tsp)
Vegetable shortening 30 g (2 tbsp)
Nonfat dry milk powder 20 g (about 2 tbsp)
Cornmeal For dusting
1. Mix the dough
• Combine the flour, instant yeast, sugar and dry milk powder.
• Add the warm water, warm milk and shortening. Mix on low speed for about 3 minutes.
• Add the salt and knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth, elastic and slightly tacky.
2. First fermentation
• Place the dough in a lightly greased bowl and cover.
• Ferment at about 78°F (26°C) for 60–75 minutes, or until roughly doubled in size.
3. Divide and shape
• Divide into 12–14 equal portions, approximately 65–75 g each.
• Shape into smooth balls, then gently flatten to about ¾ inch thick.
• Set on trays dusted with cornmeal. Dust the tops lightly with more cornmeal.
4. Final proof
• Cover loosely and proof at about 80°F (27°C) for 30–45 minutes, until noticeably puffy.
5. Cook on the griddle
• Preheat a dry griddle to 300–325°F (150–163°C).
• Cook the muffins for about 6–8 minutes per side, turning once when the first side is golden.
• Check that the centres reach approximately 200–205°F (93–96°C). If the outsides brown too quickly, lower the griddle
temperature.
6. Cool
• Transfer to wire racks and cool for at least 30 minutes before splitting or packaging.
Bakery Tips
• Use bread flour for a stronger, chewier structure.
• Dry milk powder supports flavour and browning; shortening helps keep the crumb tender.
• Keep portion weights and griddle temperature consistent for evenly sized muffins.
• Split with a fork rather than slicing with a knife to preserve the nooks and crannies.
Storage: Once completely cool, store airtight for 2–3 days or freeze for up to 3 months. Toast before serving.

title: Old-Fashioned Slow Cooker Pulled Pork
description: Makes 8–10 servings | LOW 8–10 hours | HIGH 5–6 hours DESCRIPTION Tender, juicy pork shoulder cooked slowly until it falls apart with a fork, then tossed with a homemade sweet and tangy barbecue sauce. Serve on toasted buns with coleslaw and pickles for a classic pulled pork sandwich.
ingredients:
Pork
4–5 lb (1.8–2.3 kg) pork shoulder or pork butt
1 large onion, sliced
½ cup apple cider vinegar
½ cup apple juice or water
2 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce
2 tablespoons brown sugar
1 tablespoon yellow mustard
Seasoning rub
2 teaspoons salt
2 teaspoons paprika
1 teaspoon black pepper
1 teaspoon garlic powder
1 teaspoon onion powder
½ teaspoon chili powder
Homemade barbecue sauce
1 cup ketchup
¼ cup brown sugar
¼ cup apple cider vinegar
2 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce
1 tablespoon yellow mustard
1 teaspoon smoked paprika
½ teaspoon garlic powder
¼ teaspoon black pepper
directions:
1. Prepare the pork: Pat the pork dry with paper towels. Mix the seasoning rub and rub it all over the meat.
2. Prepare the slow cooker: Place the sliced onion in the bottom. Set the pork on top.
3. Add the liquid: Mix the vinegar, apple juice (or water), Worcestershire sauce, brown sugar and mustard. Pour
around the pork.
4. Slow cook: Cover and cook on LOW for 8–10 hours or HIGH for 5–6 hours, until fork-tender. For easy
shredding, aim for about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
5. Make the barbecue sauce: Combine all barbecue sauce ingredients in a saucepan. Simmer gently for 10–15
minutes.
6. Shred the pork: Remove pork. Discard large pieces of fat and remove the bone if present. Shred with two
forks.
7. Finish: Drain excess cooking liquid, leaving a little for moisture. Stir barbecue sauce into the shredded pork to
taste.
8. Blend flavours: Return pork to the slow cooker on LOW for 20–30 minutes, then serve.
notes:
Pork shoulder gives the juiciest results.
Do not trim away all the fat before cooking; it helps keep the meat moist.
For crispy edges, spread shredded pork on a baking sheet and broil for 3–5 minutes, watching closely.
Serve on toasted buns with coleslaw and pickles.
Food safety: Whole cuts of pork should reach at least 145°F (63°C) followed by a 3-minute rest. For the tender,
pull-apart texture in this recipe, cook the shoulder longer until about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

title: Simple Sourdough for Lazy People
description: Ben Starr – The Ultimate Food Geek | March 28, 2024 Makes: 1 large loaf Hands-on prep: about 10 minutes First rise: 12–30 hours Second rise: about 90 minutes Bake: 60 minutes Oven: 425°F (220°C) DESCRIPTION An easy, no-knead sourdough loaf requiring very little hands-on work. It uses unfed sourdough starter straight from the refrigerator. No levain, stretching, folding, or complicated techniques are needed. Mix the dough, let it rise until doubled, shape, and bake in a Dutch oven starting with a cold oven.
ingredients:
113 g  unfed sourdough starter, from fridge 
340 g water
567 g all-purpose flour or bread flour
20 g salt

Oil for greasing the bowl and baking vessel
Important: Starter should be approximately 100% hydration, meaning equal weights of flour and water when feeding.
directions:
1. Mix the dough
In a large mixing bowl, combine the unfed sourdough starter and water.
Stir until the starter is distributed throughout the water.
Add the flour and salt. Stir with a spoon until the dough becomes too stiff.
Use your hand to bring everything together into a uniform dough. This should take about 15 seconds.
2. First rise
Lightly oil the mixing bowl. Return the dough to the bowl and cover.
Leave at room temperature until the dough has at least doubled in size.
This usually takes 12–30 hours, depending on starter strength and room temperature.
Do not move on until the dough has doubled.
3. Shape the loaf
Lightly flour your work surface. Remove the dough and shape it into a round loaf.
Place it into a greased Dutch oven or loaf pan.
Cover and let rise at room temperature for approximately 90 minutes.
Timing adjustments: If the first rise takes under 12 hours, the second rise may be 45–60 minutes. If the first rise takes over
30 hours, the second rise may need 120 minutes or longer.
4. Bake
Score the top of the loaf with a sharp blade or scissors.
Place the covered Dutch oven into a COLD oven .
Set the oven to 425°F (220°C). Bake covered for 45 minutes.
Remove the lid and bake another 15 minutes, until the crust is golden brown.
5. Cool
Remove the bread from the Dutch oven and place it on a cooling rack.
Allow it to cool completely before slicing.
GRANDMA'S NOTES
Do not use commercial yeast.
Do not knead or stretch and fold.
A longer first rise develops more sourdough flavour.
Do not shape before the dough doubles.
The dough can be refrigerated for up to 4 days after mixing. Allow at least 6 hours at room temperature before refrigerating,
then remove it at least 2 hours before shaping.
Source: The Ultimate Food Geek – Simple Sourdough for Lazy People

title: Butter Dip Biscuits
description: (a.k.a. Butter Swim Biscuits) Description Butter Dip Buttermilk Biscuits (also called Butter Swim Biscuits) are easy homemade biscuits. No biscuit cutter needed! They bake up thick, fluffy and buttery. Recipe Details Course: Breads, Side Dish Cuisine: American Prep Time: 10 minutes Cook Time: 25 minutes (recipe instructions allow 25–30 minutes) Total Time: 35 minutes Servings: 9 Calories: 255 kcal Author: Brandie @ The Country Cook
